name: Sara Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher from the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government. I'll keep this confidential. What fills your ordinary day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27, a senior accountant at Meridian Tax, and I lead the month-end accounts and return reviews for a cluster of clinics. I have a master's degree and a chartered accountancy qualification. I'm among the quickest there at finding a mismatch between the payroll file and the tax return, but the part I love is teaching a new accountant how to see it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do pay, savings and technology look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live alone with no children, earn more than most in this job, and have a little over a year's expenses saved. There are plenty of accounting firms nearby. I use AI every day to compare draft letters with source rules and to flag odd entries, then check its work; I like trying new systems early. I also think staff should have a voice in how a firm uses data, and clients deserve a clear right to question a machine-made decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my colleagues that the small gains are still worth measuring. A tool that catches one wrong payroll line can save a clinic a hard phone call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job and income feel secure with more than a year saved and plenty of firms nearby. I think the bigger risk here is the partners selling a harmless shortcut as a cure for everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my daily AI check against the source rules and collect a monthly tally of genuine errors caught, with the firm's permission. In the first year of a plateau I'd share the tally with staff and clients, then leave the review process alone if it adds no value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own wage. The experiment is small enough that we can put a number on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What number would make the tool useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it catches five real errors in a month without making another five, I'd keep it in the review queue. I'd show the misses too. A pretty chart can hide a bad return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who sees the tally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My team and the partners first, then clients in plain words if the firm agrees. I wouldn't publish any clinic's figures.

say: I would measure **real errors caught** by the current tool.
I would share **misses** as well as successes with the team.
think: My **job feels secure** with high pay, savings and nearby firms.
The partners could oversell a **small shortcut** to clients.
do: Keep daily **source-rule checks**; retain AI reviews only if five caught errors aren't offset by five introduced errors.
Count **real errors** monthly with firm permission.
feel: She feels **calm** about her own wage and measured experimentation.
S0.quote: A pretty chart can hide a bad return.
fieldNote: She already uses AI **every day**, so the check is current work rather than a new training plan.
Her five-error threshold includes **misses**, showing concern for evidence and client trust.

steps.text: Keep checked AI reviews if five monthly catches aren't offset by five new errors
Count real caught and missed errors monthly with firm permission

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Meridian Tax to share the gains with the people who do the checking and keep paid training open to juniors. More returns per hour should not mean silent cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The software can take much of my writing and checking, but I think I can help design a better review process. Still, if the partners stop replacing junior accountants, the team could become a thin layer of reviewers with nobody learning the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd propose a six-week paid trial on old clinic returns, with a written error log and a junior paired with me. In the first year of steady change, if the trial works, I'd ask the staff group for a meeting on trainee vacancies and a share of the time saved for paid learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the junior pipeline, although my own salary looks safe for now. I can imagine using the system without liking what happens to entry jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the junior do during the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd check the source payroll lines and mark every suggestion the system made, including the wrong ones. I'd pay attention to whether they can explain the answer without the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the partners decline paid training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the trial proposal in writing with the staff group and ask for a decision. I won't ask a junior to learn a new workflow on unpaid evenings.

say: I would ask for **paid junior training** as review work changes.
I would share **time savings** with the staff doing checks.
think: My **own salary** seems safe in the near term.
A smaller **trainee intake** could leave no one learning clinic returns.
do: Propose a **six-week paid trial** on old clinic returns.
Pair a **junior accountant** with source payroll lines and an error log.
Ask the **staff group** to discuss trainee vacancies if the trial works.
feel: She feels **uneasy** about junior jobs while her wage looks stable.
S1.quote: I won't ask a junior to learn a new workflow on unpaid evenings.
fieldNote: Her paid trial tests **explanation skill**, not just faster output, on old clinic files.
She connects junior training to **staff negotiations** over vacancies and paid time.

steps.text: Run six-week paid trial on old clinic returns if firm approves
Pair junior with payroll source checks and an error log during trial
Ask staff group to seek paid training and trainee vacancies if trial works

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that full AGI in 2028 can do our thinking work, so we need to see the fee book and a staffing plan now. I would want a public rule on who can challenge an automated tax decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own role is exposed when AGI reaches the desk in 2028, three years before robots around 2031 matter to hands-on work. I could lose a well-paid job, although a year's savings and many local firms give me room to search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the partners for the share of fees from clinic returns and add a hundred a month to my twelve-month reserve in an accessible account. In the first year after 2028, if my paid role is cut, I'd apply for posted salaried clinic-finance posts and take only paid contract reviews while searching; I'd use savings for rent, not an unfunded start-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own income for the first time in these pictures. A year of savings can cover my rent; a year of savings cannot guarantee another accountant's salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for staff without your reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the staff group's request for early notice and paid placement help before any cuts. A generous reserve makes it easier for me to argue for the people who have one month's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you launch your own AI accounts service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on the strength of a sales pitch. If the fee book says clients still pay for independent review, I'd test it after finding a wage, not spend my reserve first.

say: I would demand a **fee breakdown** and staffing plan before 2028.
I would seek a **challenge right** for automated tax decisions.
think: My **high-paid role** could disappear when AGI reaches desk work in 2028.
My **year of savings** gives search time but no guaranteed replacement wage.
do: Add **one hundred monthly** to my accessible twelve-month reserve.
Take only **paid contract reviews** while seeking posted salaried clinic-finance jobs if my role ends after 2028.
Join the **staff group** seeking early notice and paid placement help.
feel: She feels **anxious** about losing her own high salary.
S2.quote: A year of savings can cover my rent; a year of savings cannot guarantee another accountant's salary.
fieldNote: She distinguishes the **2028 desk shock** from robots three years later and rejects an unfunded start-up.
Her staff request names **paid placement**, reflecting colleagues with much thinner cushions.

steps.text: Add one hundred monthly to accessible twelve-month reserve
Apply for posted salaried clinic-finance roles if job ends after 2028
Join staff group seeking early notice and paid placement before cuts
Take only paid contract reviews while seeking work after a 2028 role cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the five-year lead time should be used to build records of where AI fails and to plan paid moves for staff. Meridian Tax should not wait until the fees fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might have changed roles by 2031, but at 32 I will still need a long career. AGI could do even the hard reviews I enjoy, so I need an income path built on actual demand, not my confidence with tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd seek a paid secondment into a clinic's finance office next year if one offers a place, and ask the firm to keep my salary while I test it. In the first year after 2031, if AGI cuts our return fees and I receive a posted salaried clinic offer, I'd move to that job; otherwise I'd keep funded review hours and apply for other posted roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but five years gives me time to learn an employer's work before deciding. Being good with AI isn't the same as having a contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a secondment teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn how a clinic sets budgets for supplies and staff, not only how its tax figures look afterward. I would need real paid work with the finance lead, not a tour of the building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you make that move without the firm's pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could afford a few weeks, but I won't ask colleagues to copy a plan only my savings make possible. I'd insist on paid time for the placement or keep my present salary.

say: I would seek a **paid clinic placement** before AGI arrives.
I would ask for **paid moves** for staff whose return work shrinks.
think: At **32 in 2031**, I still need a long income path.
AI skill does not guarantee a **salary contract** after fees fall.
do: Take a **paid clinic secondment** only if a place exists and my current salary is maintained.
Keep **funded review hours** and seek other posted roles after 2031 fee cuts if no clinic offer appears.
Accept a **posted salaried clinic offer** after 2031 if returns shrink.
feel: She feels **anxious**, though five years permits a paid trial.
S3.quote: Being good with AI isn't the same as having a contract.
fieldNote: Her clinic move requires a **paid place** and continuing salary, not just an interest in healthcare.
She uses her cushion to argue for a plan **colleagues can copy** without unpaid weeks.

steps.text: Take paid clinic secondment only if place exists and current salary is maintained
Keep funded review hours after 2031 AGI fee cuts if no clinic offer appears
Accept posted salaried clinic finance job if returns shrink after 2031
Apply for other posted salaried roles after 2031 fee cuts if no clinic offer appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues that ten years is enough to test a new service honestly and argue for rules before the deadline. I want the staff who will live with the system in the room when it is designed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 in 2036 I would still want meaningful paid work, but a decade and my savings make a transition possible. AGI reaches my desk in 2036, and robots around 2039 do not give an accountant three more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Meridian Tax for a paid, firm-owned service helping clinics audit their own AI accounts, with client fees going to the firm and a junior on paid time. I'd set a rule that at least five of eight clinics must renew at fees covering staff hours; in the first year after 2036, I'd stay if the service funds my salary, and if it does not I'd apply for posted salaried clinic finance jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy rather than alarmed. Ten years lets us collect renewal evidence and build a path before my wage is at stake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use your own savings to run it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the service belongs to Meridian Tax, and my savings are for living expenses if work changes. I'd bring the trial plan to the staff group so the junior gets paid time too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What rule would you pursue outside the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help the staff group write to the tax regulator asking for a named human appeal route on machine-prepared returns. A clinic owner should know where to take a wrong bill.

say: I would test a **firm-owned clinic audit** service with paid staff time.
I would seek a **human appeal route** for machine-made tax decisions.
think: My **desk work** is exposed in 2036 despite strong savings.
Ten years permits a **renewal test** before I depend on new fees.
do: Pilot **eight clinic audits** with firm approval and paid junior time.
Require **five of eight renewals** covering staff hours; stay after 2036 only if the service funds my salary.
Apply for **posted clinic jobs** if the firm cannot fund my salary.
feel: She feels **uneasy**, but can test paid demand over ten years.
S4.quote: A clinic owner should know where to take a wrong bill.
fieldNote: Her service is **firm-owned and salaried**, with renewal fees covering staff hours, not private side income.
She pairs the trial with a **specific regulator letter** about a human appeal route.

steps.text: Pilot eight firm-owned clinic audits with paid junior time and partner approval
Require five of eight clinic renewals covering staff hours; stay after 2036 if salary funded
Apply for posted salaried clinic finance vacancies if firm cannot fund salary
Join staff group letter requesting human tax appeal route

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because even a year of savings buys only time when fees vanish suddenly. An early fee breakdown, paid placement help and a clear appeal rule for clients would help. I want a change we can measure, not a speech we cannot pay rent with.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the first-year accountants how they will learn to catch a false number when the software hands them an answer. A senior reviewer does not appear fully trained from a download.

headlineQuote: A senior reviewer does not appear fully trained from a download.
portrait: Sara, **27**, leads clinic accounts review at Meridian Tax with a master’s degree and chartered qualification.
She earns **high pay**, lives alone, has over a year saved and many nearby accounting employers.
She uses AI **daily**, tests its errors and argues for paid junior learning and client appeal rights.
She worries most about **2028 job loss**, while longer timelines allow paid placement and measured firm service trials.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her review salary before staff and clients have a workable plan.
whatWouldHelp: An **early fee breakdown**, paid placement help and a clear client appeal route would aid the transition.
